records.title: Exploring Epigenetic Aging and Cognitive Change in Middle Adulthood
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Greater age deviation (AgeDev), in which a person’s biological age is older than their chronological age, is associated with worse cognitive performance. Most findings, however, rely on lab-administered cognitive measures and do not account for time-ordered effects of practice. The present study leveraged a measurement burst dataset to examine six distinct features of cognitive performance (peak performance, change in peak performance, intraindividual variability, forgetting, retest-related gains), and explored whether individual differences in these features can be predicted by AgeDev. In a sample of 139 adults aged 25-65, baseline AgeDev (Horvath1, Horvath2, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge), DunedinPACE, and SystemsAge were derived from DNA methylation. Across four annual high-frequency assessment bursts, processing speed and working memory were assessed via a Symbol Search and N-Back task, respectively. Using Bayesian Double Exponential Models (BDEMs), we found that baseline peak performance was lower for individuals with greater AgeDev, DunedinPACE, and chronological age. Interestingly, individuals with greater AgeDev and faster DunedinPACE showed greater retest-related gains within and across bursts. Neither AgeDev nor chronological age predicted differences in cognitive change across time. Individuals with greater AgeDev showed more intraindividual variability in processing speed. Finally, greater chronological age (but not AgeDev) was linked with more forgetting between bursts in both tasks. These findings underscore the value of multidimensional indices of cognitive performance. Importantly, even in a sample spanning young adulthood through early old age, such indices may provide unique information regarding the nature of longitudinal patterns in cognition associated with chronological or biological aging.

records.title: Impact of family video calls on depression and perceived social support among older adults residing in nursing home residents in Tabriz
records.abstract: Introduction Elderly people may need to stay in nursing home for various reasons. Separation from family may affect depression and perceived social support in older adults. This study aimed to investigate the effect of video communication on depression and perceived social support in nursing home residents.  This quasi-experimental study was conducted in 2022 on 61 older adults in nursing homes in Tabriz, Iran, using cluster sampling. Participants were randomly assigned to intervention ( n = 29) and control ( n = 32) groups. The intervention group received weekly video calls with family over two months alongside routine visits; while the Control group received routine visits only. Depression and perceived social support were assessed at baseline and after two months using Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 ( p  After the intervention, the mean depression score in intervention group was significantly lower than control group (Effect size = 0.87, p = 0.001). The mean perceived social support score (Effect size = 0.67) in the intervention group was significantly higher compared to the control (Effect size = 0.67, p = 0.01).  Video calls with family were associated with reduced depressive symptoms and increased perceived social support among nursing home residents. These findings show that video communication can be used in nursing homes to enhance the short-term well-being of residents.

records.title: Moment-to-Moment Performance and Nightly Subjective Assessments: Multi-Timescale Associations Between Subjective Age and Cognitive Function
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: An older subjective age is associated with worse cognitive health outcomes. Less is known about subjective age and cognitive function in daily life. The present study examines whether (1) baseline subjective age relates to momentary cognitive performance and nightly evaluations of subjective age and cognition, (2) daily cognitive performance relates to nightly evaluations of subjective age, and (3) nightly subjective age and cognition covary.  Participants (N = 292, age range 40-70) reported on their subjective age at baseline, completed three cognitive tasks (Dot Memory, Symbol Search, Multiple Object Tracking) three times a day, and reported their nightly subjective age and perceived cognition for eight days.  Multilevel growth models revealed that older baseline subjective age was associated with older nightly subjective age (b = 39.69, SE = 5.43, p Discussion Baseline subjective age did not relate to momentary cognitive performance, whereas both baseline levels and nightly fluctuations in subjective age were consistently linked to nightly perceptions of cognitive functioning, underscoring their relevance for understanding everyday cognitive experiences.

records.title: Life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline: a comparative qualitative study of older adults’ perspectives in Canada and Nigeria
records.abstract: Mobility is fundamental to healthy ageing and quality of life, as it enables older adults to continue participating in all spheres of life, including social, cultural, civic, spiritual, and economic activities. This study explored and compared the perspectives of Canadian and Nigerian older adults regarding life-course sociodemographic influences on mobility decline. The two distinct national contexts provided insight into mobility decline between high-income and low-resource settings shaped by unique cultural, economic, and policy environments.  We recruited eighteen Canadian and eighteen Nigerian community-dwelling older adults from diverse sociodemographic strata through community-based organisations. Using a qualitative description design, we interviewed the participants about their experiences with and observations about mobility decline. The transcripts were coded and analysed using conventional content analysis.  Of the 36 participants aged 65 to 89 years, 47.2% were women, 66.7% had a spouse or partner, and 86.1% were middle-income earners. We categorised findings into four domains: demographic, socioeconomic, sociocultural, and socioenvironmental factors. Demographic factors such as older age, ageism, women’s gender roles, and singlehood or widowhood were perceived to influence mobility decline among older adults negatively. However, most Canadian participants perceived no gender-related influence, highlighting the cultural differences in perspectives between the two groups. Socioeconomic factors (education, occupation type, and income), sociocultural factors (traditional dietary patterns, religious practices, and social participation), and socioenvironmental factors (urban versus rural living conditions, housing, and climatic challenges) were also perceived to influence the mobility trajectories of older adults. Most Canadians perceived poorer mobility among rural dwellers, while Nigerians believed the converse. We also documented the recommendations that participants made for mitigating mobility decline, including their advocacy for supportive environments and policies that recognise the unique sociodemographic contexts of older adults.  Sociodemographic factors may disproportionately influence mobility decline. Policymakers can enhance equity in ageing experiences by implementing age-friendly community initiatives that support the mobility of older adults, especially in low-resource and rural areas. records.title: Understanding the Care Priorities, Service Needs, and Lived Experiences of Rural Older Adults with Dementia and Cognitive Impairment in Canada: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: and  Research on dementia care remains largely urban-centric, with limited understanding about the lived experiences and needs of people with cognitive impairment and dementia in rural communities. This scoping review aimed to understand the care priorities, service needs, and lived experiences of rural older adults with cognitive impairment and dementia in Canada. Research Design and  Following Arksey and O’Malley’s scoping review framework, we searched CINAHL, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science for journal articles published from January 2015 to January 2025. Two reviewers independently screened the articles and extracted data from the relevant articles. We used reflexive thematic analysis to analyze the data.  The scoping review identified 616 initial articles, with 16 relevant studies included in our review. Four interconnected themes were identified: i) complex navigational pathways and barriers in rural dementia care; ii) limited dementia knowledge creates challenges across the disease trajectory; iii) gaps in access to dementia-related services and supports; and iv) dementia-related stigma, fear, and social isolation.  The findings revealed critical challenges in navigating rural dementia care, where geographical distance, misinformation, limited services, and dementia-related stigma exacerbate cognitive care disparities. Addressing these challenges requires ingenuity and prioritizing lived experience research to inform community-relevant solutions. Strategic investment and implementation science are needed to co-design, implement, and evaluate navigational support models and interdisciplinary dementia care hubs to improve rural access. Advancing rural dementia care requires moving beyond documenting challenges to evaluating scalable population-level interventions.

records.title: Rationale, Design, and Baseline Characteristics of the TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) Cohort of Older Adults for Assessing Fall and Fracture Risk: Prospective Cohort Study
records.abstract: Falls and fractures are a major clinical concern for older adults. International clinical guidelines recommend annual fall risk screening for all adults aged 60 years and older. However, existing falls risk–screening algorithms have shown limited sensitivity and specificity in detecting future falls. Emerging health technologies, including wearable sensors, in-silico finite element models (FEMs), and virtual reality (VR) technology, show promise in enhancing fall and fracture risk assessments by providing more personalized  data to support targeted primary prevention. However, large-scale longitudinal studies are required to evaluate their predictive accuracy and cost-effectiveness for systematic community–based screening.  The TARGET (Targeted Assessment and Recruitment of Geriatrics for Effective Fall Prevention Treatments) study is an ongoing national prospective cohort study in Singapore designed to develop cost-effective and scalable frameworks for the early detection and prevention of falls and fractures using novel health technologies. This paper describes the rationale, design, and baseline characteristics of TARGET, and provides preliminary insights into how these novel technologies perform in discriminating between older adults with and with no history of falls at study baseline.  A total of 2291 community-dwelling Singapore residents aged ≥60 years were enrolled between 2022 and 2024. Participants underwent a comprehensive baseline fall risk assessment comprising (1) home-based interview to assess sociodemographic, anthropometric, cognitive, physical, functional, and psychosocial status; (2) gait assessment using wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) motion sensors; (3) dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and whole-body 3D scans to construct subject-specific FEMs; and (4) VR-based cognitive assessment to probe spatial navigation deficits. Prospective follow-up for 2 years is ongoing, with linkage to national electronic medical records (EMRs) to obtain detailed clinical, medication, and pathological data.  Of the total cohort, 58% (1327/2291) were female, with a mean age of 74.6 years at baseline. TARGET represents a relatively healthy older adult population, with 83% (1898/2291) remaining fully independent, 44% (1016/2290) with mild cognitive impairment, 50% (440/879) with osteopenia, and 15% (358/2291) reporting falls in the past year. Significant baseline functional, psychosocial, cognitive, and biomechanical differences were identified between fallers and nonfallers. Fallers had poorer physical and psychosocial health, greater gait variability, and a higher risk of osteoporotic fractures. Novel risk prediction models integrating epidemiological, IMUs, FEM, VR, and EMR data are in development and being validated against gold standard clinical assessments, with cost-effectiveness evaluations of the economic feasibility of adopting these screening measures at scale.  Leveraging comprehensive epidemiological, EMR, and health technology data, TARGET is well positioned to identify novel biomarkers and systemic interactions that may predict falls and fracture risk, with potential application to other age-related diseases with shared pathophysiology. In particular, TARGET’s focus on community-based screening using technologies that can be administered by nonclinical personnel has the potential to reduce substantial burden and costs within the health care sector.

records.title: Workplace Violence in Home Health: Staff and Leadership Experiences and Strategies
records.abstract: and  Workplace violence (WPV) in healthcare has increased over the last decade, yet limited evidence exists to guide home health agency (HHA) prevention efforts. This study examined HHA leaders and staff WPV experiences, including the type of violence, risk factors, and prevention strategies. Research Design and  We conducted one-on-one semi-structured phone interviews with a purposive HHA sample of (a) 105 leaders, each representing a different organization, between November 2020-December 2022 and (b) 28 staff from five agencies between April 2023-August 2025. The socioecological framework guided the thematic analysis.  Leaders and staff contrasted the solitary, uncontrolled, and unpredictable HHA work environment with institutional healthcare contexts. HHA staff experiences reflected three types of WPV (i.e., criminal intent, violence perpetrated by the patient or others in the home, ideological violence perpetrated by the public). WPV risk factors spanned all domains of the socioecological framework. HHA staff and leaders described individual- and organizational-level WPV prevention strategies that targeted risk factors across framework domains. There was an absence of prevention strategies initiated at the community- and societal-level (e.g., WPV prevention legislation). Organizational strategies extended beyond annual staff training to include patient-specific safety plans, employing safety escorts, and discharge protocols for patient non-compliance with safety plans.  Fostering HHA staff safety within the context of service delivery is complex and multi-dimensional. Findings emphasized the importance of a comprehensive approach that is tailored to the HHA’s community and populations served and a need for societal-level policies addressing WPV prevention and mitigation.

records.title: Healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning related to mealtimes in long-term care facilities: an interview study
records.abstract: Mealtimes in long-term care facilities are complex and serve multiple purposes. They provide opportunities for participation and learning, involving residents, relatives and healthcare professionals, each with unique circumstances. Participation and learning are central to healthy ageing. Healthcare professionals play a key role in enabling participation and learning among those involved, although these opportunities may be shaped by their perceptions and attitudes. Therefore, this study aimed to explore healthcare professionals’ perceptions of participation and learning among residents, their relatives, and colleagues related to mealtime situations in long-term care facilities.  Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews with 23 healthcare professionals (nursing assistants, licensed practical nurses, and registered nurses) working in long-term care facilities in a municipality in south-eastern Sweden. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.  Three themes were generated: (1) Shaped by relationships and circumstances , (2) Rewarding yet challenging , and (3) Prerequisites influence opportunities. Participation and learning related to mealtime situations manifested in various ways and to differing degrees, from extensive to almost non-existent. It was a balancing act for the healthcare professionals managing multiple challenges to enable participating and learning; however, residents and relatives were seldom invited to engage in this problem-solving. For participation and learning to occur, prerequisites were required at all levels in the organisation.  Healthcare professionals perceive that participation and learning among residents, relatives, and colleagues in long-term care facilities do occur, but to varying degrees and are associated with multiple challenges. Drawing on a learning model, such as Illeris, can help identify which components need to be developed, which together with a deeper understanding and implementation of person-centredness, could contribute to increased participation and learning, and thereby to the wellbeing of residents, relatives, and healthcare professionals. However, this approach must permeate the entire organisation.

records.title: Impact of supervised physical exercise on inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
records.abstract: and  Physical exercise is widely recognized as an effective non-pharmacological intervention that improves not only functional capacity, but also cognition and quality of life in older adults. However, the molecular pathways through which it influences aging-related processes remain incompletely understood. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize current evidence on the effects of structured physical exercise intervention on molecular biomarkers associated with inflammation and oxidative stress in older adults. Research Design and  Randomized controlled trials which included participants ≥65 years old were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Library.  A total of 50 reports (4,379 participants) were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 38 of them in the different meta-analyses performed. Exercise interventions ranged from 8 weeks to 12 months and included aerobic, resistance, and multicomponent training. Pooled analyses indicated modest but significant reductions in C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and high-sensitivity CRP, as well as increases in IL-10. Effects on other pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 and TNF-α, were inconsistent across studies. Evidence from a limited number of trials (n = 6) also suggested improvements in redox balance.  Overall, structured physical exercise demonstrates a moderate immunomodulatory and antioxidant effect in older adults, although bias was moderate to high. PROSPERO registry: CRD420251006248.

records.title: Physical Performance and Daytime Sleepiness as Correlates of Life-Space Mobility in Community-Dwelling Older Adults
records.abstract: Life-space mobility reflects the extent and independence with which older adults move within their environments and is an integrative indicator of functional capacity and social participation. records.title: Understanding the Benefits of Textiles in Facilitating Interactions for People With Dementia: An Exploration of Design Considerations and Recommendations
records.abstract: As the global population of people with dementia increases, the demand for best practice dementia care is growing. Textiles have the potential to assist with interacting with people with dementia and provide benefits in dementia care settings. However, there is currently limited understanding of, or experience with, the specific challenges, considerations and design of interactive textile products for people with moderate to advanced dementia. This exploratory qualitative study aimed to explore the perspectives of using interactive textiles with people with dementia. Seven sets of interactive textiles were tested for usability with nine people with dementia, followed by post-testing interviews. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with care partners and healthcare professionals to understand the effects of interactive textiles in two care settings. In total, 27 people were interviewed, including people with dementia ( n = 9), informal care partners ( n = 5), formal care partners/staff ( n = 2), and healthcare professionals ( n = 11), from a residential care home, a daycare centre, and a university located in southeastern Australia. The findings highlighted several benefits of interactive textiles, including assisting interactions, facilitating communication, providing sensory stimulation, supporting reminiscence, and promoting positive emotions such as reducing stress and anxiety. Participants suggest textiles can be used to provide engagement, describing the importance of forging connections between people with dementia and their past, bolstering familiar associations, emotional relations, and recognition of personal preferences. These insights informed design considerations and recommendations for creating interactive textiles that offer playful and meaningful activities for people with dementia.

records.title: Service use after long-term care entry: low utilization and early dropout in Taiwan
records.abstract: and  Home- and community-based services (HCBS) are central to Taiwan’s long-term care (LTC) system, yet some users show limited service use after entering the system. This study examined predictors of two patterns of limited HCBS use: low utilization and early dropout. Research Design and  This study analyzed administrative LTC records from Pingtung County, Taiwan, among cases entering the LTC system during 2019–2021: 17,517 in the low-utilization analysis and 18,678 in the early-dropout analysis. Low utilization was defined as service use in the lowest quartile of service-use days per 30 follow-up days, and early dropout as case closure within 90 days. Bootstrap-enhanced least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (BoLASSO) was applied, followed by multivariable logistic regression.  Low utilization was associated with care arrangements and entry pathways, including institutional residence, use of a paid migrant caregiver, co-residence with a nonfamily caregiver, and entry via the 1966 hotline. Early dropout occurred in 11.4% of cases and was associated with cancer, oxygen-related care needs, severe pain, underweight, unintentional weight loss, and inability to complete short-term memory assessment. Service-provider referral was associated with lower odds of both outcomes.  Low utilization and early dropout showed distinct predictor patterns: the former was more closely associated with care resources and entry pathways, whereas the latter was associated with health instability and recent decline. Distinguishing these patterns may inform more tailored care management and service delivery based on users’ needs and care contexts.

records.title: Relationship Quality Trajectories and Financial Abuse Among Older Adults
records.abstract: and  Financial abuse is a prevalent yet underreported form of elder abuse with serious health and economic consequences. Prior research has linked poor relationship quality to financial abuse risk, but most studies rely on cross-sectional designs and focus on a single relationship type. This study examined whether 10-year changes in relationship quality with spouses, family, and friends are associated with subsequent financial abuse. Research Design and  Guided by social exchange theory, this study used data from three waves of the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project. Relationship quality was categorized as stable, improving, or worsening over a 10-year period. Logistic regression models were estimated for each relationship type, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics.  Older adults with worsening family or friendship relationships over the 10-year period had more than twice the odds of experiencing subsequent financial abuse compared with those with stable relationships. Improving relationship trajectories were not significantly associated with financial abuse risk. Changes in spousal relationship quality were also not significantly associated with financial abuse.  These findings suggest that worsening family and friendship relationships over time may be an early indicator of financial abuse risk. Monitoring changes in older adults’ social relationships and supporting relationship stability may be important strategies for preventing financial abuse in later life.

records.title: Multimodal Dementia Prediction With Large Language Models: Cross-Attention Over Text, Audio, and Image
records.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is a leading cause of dementia, and there is growing interest in scalable approaches for early screening using speech-based tasks. While prior work has demonstrated promising  using either transcript-based language features or acoustic cues, most approaches remain unimodal or rely on simple fusion strategies that do not explicitly consider interactions across modalities.  In this study, we propose an attention-based trimodal fusion framework that integrates text, audio, and image representations of the Cookie Theft picture, which serves as the shared visual stimulus in the picture-description task.  Our method uses a new bidirectional cross-attention mechanism to achieve a unified multimodal embedding for downstream tasks. We evaluate the approach on 2 tasks: AD detection by classifying whether the participant has AD or not, and AD severity assessment by predicting Mini-Mental Status Examination cognitive scores.  On the AD detection task, trimodal fusion achieves the best overall performance ( F 1 -score=0.8667, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.9032), outperforming unimodal baselines, bimodal fusion, and conventional early or late fusion . For AD severity assessment, the proposed multimodal representation reduces prediction error of root mean squared error to about 4.20, improving over both unimodal and bimodal fusion settings. We further perform the ablation analysis to show that bidirectional cross-attention consistently outperforms conventional unidirectional cross-attention.  These  demonstrate that attention-based multimodal fusion can enhance dementia prediction from picture-description responses and provide a strong foundation for developing multimodal cognitive screening pipelines.

records.title: Tailored personas for home-based fall prevention among older adults with stroke: A qualitative study
records.abstract: and  Existing home-based fall prevention strategies often adopt a one-size-fits-all approach despite substantial heterogeneity among older adults with stroke. Persona-based  may facilitate more individualized intervention design, yet remain largely unexplored in stroke rehabilitation. This study explored variations in fall prevention self-management among older adults with stroke and developed user personas to represent their diverse experiences, challenges, and support needs. Research Design and  A qualitative descriptive study was conducted among 26 older adults with stroke receiving home-based care in China. Participants were recruited using purposive maximum-variation sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and March 2026. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify key dimensions of fall prevention self-management. Individual participant profiles were iteratively synthesized through cross-case comparison into composite personas representing recurring configurations of behaviors, beliefs, barriers, resources, and support needs.  Five distinct personas emerged: proactive self-managers, risk-discounting managers, routine-based managers, support-constrained managers, and professionally supported managers. These personas demonstrated distinct combinations of fall-risk perception, social resources, environmental constraints, and healthcare dependence.  The findings demonstrate substantial diversity in how older adults with stroke manage fall prevention in home settings. Persona-based stratification provides an actionable approach for designing scalable, context-sensitive fall prevention interventions.

records.title: Developing hybrid nudges to promote mental health help-seeking in Chinese older adults: A co-design approach
records.abstract: and  Older adults often face significant barriers to mental health help-seeking. This study integrated participatory co-design with behavioural science principles to develop culturally meaningful hybrid nudges to normalise mental health help-seeking among older adults in Hong Kong. Research Design and  Twelve older adults with mental health volunteering experience participated in eight researcher-facilitated co-design workshops structured by design thinking principles. A graphic designer assisted in visualising the prototypes. Workshop artefacts, design outputs, structured summaries, and focus group recordings were analysed using thematic analysis. The study was primarily an intervention development study; focus group data were used as an embedded process evaluation to understand participants’ experiences of co-design.  Co-designers were 75% female with a mean age of 63.83 years. The co-design process produced a set of hybrid nudge prototypes with two design orientations: (1) reminiscence-oriented using metaphors from childhood games to cue autonomy and peer support, and (2) psychoeducation-oriented using relatable vignettes to model perspective taking. Although the project initially aimed to create social norms and visual nudges, co-designers preferred integrating brief psychoeducational and general well-being content to increase acceptability. The embedded process evaluation highlighted perceived learning, ownership, and collaboration, as well as challenges such as self-doubt.  Participatory co-design can support the development of theory-informed and culturally attuned hybrid nudges to address motivational barriers to mental health help-seeking. Future research should test acceptability and behavioural outcomes through randomized or pragmatic trials, and examine how to balance theoretical fidelity with participant agency in co-designed behavioural interventions.

records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Atypical survey response patterns, such as inconsistent or implausible responses, have been linked to lower cognitive functioning in later life. Extreme responding was not significantly associated with dementia risk. Secondary analyses suggested stronger associations among individuals younger than 75 years and those with higher levels of education. Discussion Routine survey responses contain behavioral signals associated with emerging dementia risk. Because these indicators can be derived from existing survey data without additional testing burden, they may provide a scalable complement to traditional approaches for studying cognitive aging in large population-based cohorts.

records.title: Is there a role for artificial intelligence in end-of-life care for persons with dementia? Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff
records.abstract: and  Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families’ and staff’s acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia. Design and  In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.  Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants’ narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.  Families and frontline staff should not be considered merely as end users, but as key stakeholders whose needs and expertise should shape the direction of AI applications.

records.title: Approach to sarcopenia in older adults: a systematic review of dietary and exercise interventions in the primary care setting
records.abstract: / Population aging presents challenges for society and healthcare, notably in preventing sarcopenia, a condition that impairs older adults’ quality of life and functionality. This article reviews the current literature on dietary and exercise interventions to evaluate their effectiveness in managing sarcopenia and explore their integration in primary care.  A systematic review was conducted under PRISMA guidelines by searching PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Embase, and the Cochrane Library via MeSH terms and the PICOS criteria. The analysis focused on randomized studies involving adults over 65 years of age that assessed nutritional and exercise interventions delivered in primary care settings.  Six studies, encompassing 444 participants in experimental groups and 226 in control groups, met the inclusion criteria. Combined interventions, physical exercise paired with nutritional supplementation, demonstrated notable improvements in muscle strength, physical function, and body composition. However, the  varied depending on the study design and adherence rates.  Multidimensional approaches within primary care show promising potential for slowing sarcopenia progression and enhancing quality of life among older adults. Despite encouraging findings, limited research in this area signals the need for further studies emphasizing personalized, sustainable strategies to optimize clinical implementation.

records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: Aging is accompanied by changes in body composition and cognition. Although adiposity has been linked to metabolic dysfunction and dementia risk, associations with specific cognitive domains in later life remain unclear.  This cross-sectional study examined associations between adiposity and cognitive performance in 769 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (70–94 years) from the Study of Muscle, Mobility and Aging (SOMMA). Adiposity was assessed using anthropometric measures (body mass index, waist circumference) and MRI-derived regional fat volumes, including visceral and abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue. Cognitive performance was evaluated using a screening measure (Montreal Cognitive Assessment), processing speed (Digit Symbol Coding Test), executive function (Trail Making Test B), and memory (California Verbal Learning Test–II Short Form). Multivariable linear regression models were sequentially adjusted for demographic, cardiometabolic, psychosocial, and behavioral factors.  Greater age was associated with lower adiposity and poorer cognitive performance (p  In healthy older adults, adiposity is most consistently related to processing speed, whereas associations with memory and executive function are weaker or absent. Processing speed may be especially sensitive to adiposity-related differences. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal relationships.

records.title: Associations between social network characteristics and daily social experiences in later life: Evidence from ecological momentary assessment
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Sociological theory posits that social networks function as enduring relational structures that constrain and enable everyday social interactions, yet empirical evidence linking network properties to real-time social exposures remains limited. To address this gap, this study examines how older adults' social networks are associated with their daily social experiences.  Using data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas (SECHURA) study, we combine egocentric network data (1,474 alters from 254 respondents) with ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data capturing real-time social interactions over one week (5,342 observations). We evaluate associations between three network properties–structure (quantity, composition, and interconnectedness of network members), heterogeneity (diversity in gender, race/ethnicity, and age), and strength (strong and supportive ties) – and four momentary outcomes (number and type of interaction partners, social activities, and being outside the home).  Random-effects models show that larger and more socially diverse networks are associated with greater momentary social engagement, including more interaction partners, less time alone, and more explicit socializing. Both role diversity and network density are associated with heightened social exposure, through distinct pathways. Sociodemographic heterogeneity also predicts interaction patterns, with age heterogeneity linked to kin-centered interactions and racial heterogeneity to non-kin exposure. Stronger affective ties predicted less engagement in explicit socializing. Discussion Personal social networks operate as critical structures linked to the quantity, composition, and context of older adults' real-time social exposures. Large, densely connected, and role-diverse networks appear to facilitate everyday interactions through different mechanisms.

records.title: The modifying effect of work-care role conflict on the effectiveness of carer support: Results from the Australian Draw Care randomised clinical trial
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
records.abstract: People who care for a family member with dementia alongside paid work often experience role conflict. This study explores whether work-care role conflict (WCRC) modifies the effectiveness of Draw Care, an online and culturally-adapted carer support intervention.  Secondary exploratory analysis of a single-blind, parallel-group trial (August 2023–November 2024) that compared Draw Care against waitlist control in adult carers from diverse linguistic backgrounds. To formally test whether WCRC moderated the effect of the Draw-Care intervention, we ran a full-sample linear mixed model that included a three-way interaction between time-point, treatment group and an indicator of WCRC. WCRC was operationalised as self-report of missed work or reduced productivity due to competing care and employment demands. Outcomes included carer burden, mood, quality of life, and productivity/ activity impairment at 6 and 12 weeks.  Forty-two of 93 carers reported WCRC. Reductions in caregiver burden due to treatment at 6 weeks (-10.00; 95% CI -19.70 to -0.31, p = 0.043) and 12 weeks (-9.56; 95% CI -18.83 to -0.29, p = 0.043) were significantly larger in participants with WCRC than without. This moderating effect of WCRC was driven by a robust, absolute reduction in caregiver burden in intervention group participants with WCRC over the initial 6 weeks (-7.19, 95%CI: -12.72 to -1.67, p = 0.011), with much of this improvement preserved at 12 weeks (-6.85, 95%CI: -12.17 to -1.53, p = 0.012).  WCRC appears to modify the effectiveness of Draw Care, suggesting that the intervention may be particularly helpful for carers navigating role conflict.

records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: This study investigates the influence of respondents’ and informants’ gender on informants’ assessments of cognitive functioning in population studies in the United States and Mexico.  Using data from the Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS-HCAP) (N = 3,025) in the United States and the Mexican Cognitive Aging Study (Mex-Cog) (N = 1071) in Mexico, we examined informant reports of cognitive decline with 17 questions from the Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSI-D). Female informants in the United States reported 0.57 more CSI-D symptoms compared to male informants while in Mexico they reported 1.35 fewer symptoms. Discussion Our  show that informant gender is associated with systematically different reporting patterns depending on the national and cultural context in which the assessment takes place. The  suggest that informant reports of cognitive decline may represent social norms in addition to actual cognitive decline.

records.title: There must be fifty ways to reduce ageism: A theoretical perspective on possible interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism among older persons
records.abstract: Ageism is defined as stereotypes, prejudices, and discrimination toward people because of their age. It represents a substantial public health concern given its high prevalence and extensive impact on the health and well-being of older persons. Although interventions to reduce ageism toward older persons among younger persons as agents of ageism exist, much less is known about interventions to reduce self- and other-directed ageism toward older persons among older persons. This theoretical paper addresses the gap by proposing a comprehensive framework for the development of interventions to reduce ageism among older persons in the second half of life. Drawing on established theories, such as contact theory, terror management theory, stereotype embodiment theory, and social identity theory, we propose various mechanisms through which ageism among older persons can be reduced. The paper explores theoretical assumptions about which interventions work for whom and why to guide further empirical research on the reduction of ageism in the second half of life. We argue that although at the present time, effective interventions to reduce ageism among older persons are scarce, there are many theoretical avenues that may prove effective.

records.title: Development and Validation of the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) Scale: A Three-Study Investigation of Perceived Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism in Clinical Care
records.abstract: and  Ageism in healthcare contributes to undertreatment, dismissive communication, and age-based exclusions from care, yet no psychometrically validated, patient-reported measure captures older adults’ perceptions of age-based bias during clinical encounters. We developed and validated the Attitudes Toward Healthcare Providers (ATHP) scale. Research Design and  Items adapted from four validated discrimination measures plus two new items were administered to community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older in three independent, predominantly non-Hispanic White samples (Ns = 223, 349, 361) recruited through Prolific within the United States. Study 1 examined latent structure with exploratory factor analysis; Study 2 tested and refined the structure with confirmatory factor analysis; Study 3 confirmed the refined model and evaluated reliability, measurement invariance across gender, and construct validity.  Study 1 identified two correlated factors, Interpersonal and Institutional Ageism, corroborated by parallel analysis and Velicer’s MAP test. Study 2 indicated that a 20-item model fit poorly and that removing three items produced a refined 17-item model. Study 3 confirmed this model (CFI = .926, RMSEA = .058, SRMR = .057), with excellent reliability for Interpersonal Ageism and the total scale, good reliability for Institutional Ageism, full scalar invariance across gender, and coherent discriminant and convergent validity.  The 17-item ATHP is a psychometrically sound, healthcare-specific measure distinguishing interpersonal from institutional ageism, equipping researchers, health systems, and policymakers to monitor age-based bias and evaluate interventions.

records.title: Mapping Namaste Care Training for Staff in Long-Term Care Settings: A Scoping Review
records.abstract: Namaste Care is a person-centered intervention for people with dementia in long-term care, particularly those in advanced stages. However, evidence on how staff are trained and supported to deliver Namaste Care remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map training content, delivery formats and support, and training-related outcomes. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, eight databases were searched from inception to May 2026, with additional website and citation searches. Data were synthesized descriptively, and training-related outcomes were mapped against the Kirkpatrick Four-Level Training Evaluation Model. Eleven studies were included. Training commonly addressed core Namaste Care principles and activities, and several programs also included knowledge of dementia and palliative care, as well as communication and relational care skills. Face-to-face workshops and in-service sessions were the most common delivery formats, with some programs also incorporating experiential learning. Follow-up support and practical resources were frequently reported, and family involvement was incorporated into several programs. Staff reactions were generally positive. Learning-related outcomes included greater understanding of the purpose and delivery of Namaste Care and reported improvements in knowledge, attitudes, and self-perceived skills. Some studies reported changes in staff practice, although intended program frequency or duration was not always achieved because of staffing and organizational constraints. Resident, staff, and family caregiver outcomes were mixed and could not be attributed to training alone. Namaste Care training is therefore better understood as part of a broader practice-support strategy rather than as a stand-alone educational activity. However, existing evaluations remain incomplete, with limited evidence linking staff learning to subsequent practice change and wider outcomes.

records.title: Living Arrangements and Life Without and With Depression in Japan: A Longitudinal Analysis
records.abstract: This study examines how life expectancy (LE) without and with depression differs by living arrangement among older adults in Japan, with particular attention to gender differences.  Data were drawn from the Nihon University Japanese Longitudinal Study of Aging (1999–2009). Multistate life table  were used to estimate LE spent without and with depression among adults aged 65 years and older across different living arrangements.  Pronounced gender differences were observed in the relationship between living arrangements and depression-based health expectancy. Men living alone experienced the longest duration and the highest proportion of their remaining lives with depression, whereas among women, these patterns were observed among those living with their spouse. Discussion Living arrangements shape depression-based health expectancy differently for older men and women in Japan, highlighting the need for gender-sensitive policies that address the social contexts in which they are embedded.

records.title: Personal networks and cognitive health across rural-urban contexts
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Prior research often reports geographic cognitive health disparities in later life, including across rural-urban contexts. Yet few studies have examined the role of personal social networks in shaping these geographic disparities. This study investigates whether social networks moderate or mediate the association between geographic context and cognitive health.  We use data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study, which is a state representative sample of adults aged 55 and older. A latent measure of social bridging (i.e., connections to weak and diverse ties) was extracted using personal network data. Cognitive health was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Rurality was defined using the Indiana County Classification. Moderation and mediation pathways were tested using linear regression models.  There were no observed rural-urban differences in MoCA scores. Yet the association between social bridging and MoCA was significantly stronger among rural participants compared to urban participants. Rural participants with the lowest levels of social bridging performed significantly worse on the MoCA compared to urban participants with similar bridging levels. These geographic disparities were not present when comparing rural and urban participants with high levels of social bridging. Discussion The ability to personally bridge social ties within a network appears to play a more critical role in the cognitive health of rural residents, who live in communities with fewer structural opportunities for social stimulation, compared to urban residents.

records.title: Bridge jobs and retirement identities: Gendered life course approach to workforce exits among Early Boomers
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: The prevalence of bridge jobs, post-career work that bridges between career jobs and workforce exit, has obfuscated the isomorphic link between older adults’ role identities as retirees, named ‘retirement identities’, and their actual labor force status in ways that may well differ by gender. We examine how gender and Social Security eligibility/receipt are associated with retirement identities, and how these identities are associated with the timing of final workforce exit.  We track bridge job take-ups and workforce exits of Early Boomers (ages 51-56 in 2004, N = 910) in the Health and Retirement Study 2004-2020. We use multinomial logistic regression to examine predictors of retirement identities by gender, and event history analysis to examine the timing of workforce exit at the intersection of gender, retirement identity, and timing of bridge job take-up.  Findings reveal that Social Security receipt is associated with men’s retirement identity formation, but not women’s. For both genders, ordered retirement identities, from ‘not retired’ to ‘completely retired,’ predict the timing of workforce exits. Women in bridge jobs do not always exit the workforce earlier than men when retirement identities are taken into account. Discussion This study underscores the changes in retirement as an institutionalized and gendered life course status passage, amplified by the increasing pivoting to bridge jobs, but with considerable variability in self-definitions of retirement status. Our evidence suggests that these identities serve as good signals of older workers’ work attachments and retirement plans, offering helpful insights for policymakers and employers.

records.title: Dyadic discrimination and mental well-being among older Americans
records.abstract: and  There is a thorough literature on the mental health consequences of discrimination exposure in adulthood, yet little work to date has situated such experiences within a relational, dyadic context. The present brief report analyzes two-wave longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS; 2018-2022) to determine whether individuals’ own or their intimate partner’s experiences of discrimination were associated with changes to anxiety symptoms, perceived stress, and/or self-esteem over a four-year period. Research  and Design Dyadic lagged dependent variable (LDV) models were estimated using a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework with full information maximum likelihood (FIML)  to address missing data. A total of 1,484 individuals from 742 opposite-gender couples participated at both the 2018 and 2022 waves of data collection and comprised the analytic sample for this study.  Individuals’ own exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased symptoms of anxiety and perceived stress, as well as with reduced self-esteem, over the four-year period. A dyadic partner’s exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased anxiety symptoms for men only, though post-hoc Wald tests failed to find a significant gender difference in effects.  Discrimination is a chronic psychosocial stressor with harmful consequences for mental health of affected individuals even in mid and later life. Moreover, limited evidence suggests that discrimination may have dyadic consequences as well, though these patterns are mixed. Future research is needed to determine interpersonal mechanisms for the findings of interest.

records.title: Caregiver Burden and Associated Factors Among Family Caregivers of People With Dementia in Rural and Remote Areas: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
records.abstract: Evidence on family caregivers of people with dementia in rural and remote areas remains limited, and burden levels and associated factors lack systematic quantitative synthesis.  To synthesize burden and associated factors.  Nine databases were searched through November 2025 following PRISMA. Quality was appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Comparable data were meta-analyzed; others were narratively synthesized.  Twelve studies involving 1,416 caregivers were included. Pooled mean scores were 45.19 for the 22-item Zarit Burden Interview (95% CI 29.49–60.89) and 19.90 for the 12-item version (95% CI 12.98–26.82). Burden was associated with behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia ( r = 0.44, 95% CI 0.16–0.65), poorer caregiver mental health ( r = 0.48, 95% CI 0.38–0.56), and longer dementia or caregiving duration ( r = 0.29, 95% CI 0.13–0.43). Narrative synthesis implicated functional impairment, greater caregiving demands, lower self-efficacy, and economic disadvantage. Despite low-to-very-low certainty, findings indicate substantial, multifactorial burden and prioritize caregiver support. PROSPERO CRD420261277658.

records.title: The bidirectional relationship between depression and cognitive function in older adults: Evidence from a psychosocial intervention on late-life depression
records.abstract: and  Depression is a modifiable predictor of dementia, but the effects of addressing depression to improve cognition, especially psychosocial interventions, are understudied. The underlying relationships between depressive symptoms (DS) and cognitive function (CF) are also unclear. Most prior research has been observational, lacking insight into their interactions during interventions. This study examined the longitudinal relationships between DS and CF across psychosocial interventions in older adults, modeling changes as latent variables for more accurate estimations. Research Design and  The study drew on participant data from JC JoyAge, a community stepped-care program for late-life mental health. Participants (≥60 years) with mild to moderate DS (N = 4,412) completed DS and CF assessments (e.g., attention, language, orientation, memory domains) before and after the program. Latent change score models were computed to examine changes in DS and CF as well as their interaction.  On average, participants’ DS and CF improved following intervention. A greater reduction in DS was associated with greater improvement in CF. Higher baseline CF predicted a greater reduction in DS, while a lower baseline DS predicted a greater improvement in global CF, attention, and memory.  The findings demonstrated the bidirectional relationships between DS and CF and showed their shared improvements during psychosocial intervention. Treating depression is expected to benefit cognition, potentially preventing cognitive decline and dementia. Combining depression and cognition components in integrated intervention approaches may enhance their reciprocal response. Early intervention at a lower depression level may achieve greater cognitive benefits.

records.title: Mapping heterogeneity in retirement transition pathways: Integrating qualitative longitudinal and text mining analysis
records.abstract: and  Retirement transition (RT) is a dynamic process with individual heterogeneity. While the Resource-Based Dynamic Perspective (RBDP) highlights fluctuations in key resources, studies remain largely quantitative and cross-sectional. This study aims to identify distinct RT patterns and examine shifts in resource-related discourse over time. Research Design and  A qualitative longitudinal design with computational augmentation tracked 12 Taiwanese near-retirees across five waves spanning six months pre- to six months post-retirement. Sixty qualitative transcripts were analyzed using longitudinal case , complemented by computational text mining (Sentence-BERT) to trace trajectories across six resource domains, including Health Issues, Life Control, Financial Status, Social Support, Emotional Response, and Lifestyle.  Within this sample, three analytically derived RT patterns were observed: a transition-centered pattern in Strategic Goal-Driven (Type I, n = 4), a U-shaped pattern in Structure and Social Role Reshaping (Type II, n = 4), and a crisis-driven peak in External Shock Response (Type III, n = 4). Text-mining  broadly converged with qualitative findings, particularly in the Life Control domain. At the individual level, convergence was observed for financial status and lifestyle, whereas divergence emerged when similar quantitative frequencies corresponded to different qualitative meanings.  Findings extend RBDP by introducing resource diversion, in which family or contextual demands redirect personal resources, and a resource hierarchy highlighting the foundational role of physical health. Findings underscore the need for pathway-specific retirement support that accounts for culturally embedded caregiving obligations beyond conventional financial-planning approaches.
